intro: Variation XII, “B.G.N.” (Andante), from Elgar’s Variations on an Original Theme “Enigma”, Op. 36, is a portrait of Basil Nevinson, who was the cellist in Elgar’s piano trio. A solo cello opens and closes the variation.

sections.label: Var 12 · Andante, Nevinson’s solo cello
sections.mNote: Solo cello plays over soft lower strings.

sections.label: Var 12 · Violins join the cello melody
sections.mNote: Divided violins play above the cello phrase.

sections.label: Var 12 · Andante, solo cello
sections.mNote: The orchestra thins out around the solo cello.

cues.title: Solo cello, rehearsal 52
cues.text: A solo cello begins molto espressivo and ad libitum for its first two bars, accompanied by quiet violas and the other cellos. At a tempo the whole cello section takes up the tune, marked largamente ed espressivo.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 82, rehearsal 52: solo cello marked molto espressivo and ad libitum, followed by a tempo and largamente ed espressivo for the cello section.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nevinson, cellist in Elgar’s trio
cues.text: Nevinson played chamber music with Elgar on violin and Hew David Steuart-Powell at the piano. In his written tribute Elgar praised his playing and recorded that Nevinson put his scientific and artistic skills at his friends’ disposal, wholeheartedly.
cues.evidence: Elgar, My Friends Pictured Within (Novello, 1946), commentary on variation XII, reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations. The Elgar Society confirms the trio: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: Ending for solo cello
cues.text: The orchestra makes a diminuendo, and the solo cello has the last phrase. After a long pause the cello rises once more over held lower strings. The final marking is attacca, and the Romanza follows without a break.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 86: diminuendo molto, solo cello, longa fermata, ritardando and attacca. The extra final bar is reserved for separate performances.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Wind releases under the solo cello
transitions.from: Var 12 · Violins join the cello melody
transitions.how: Elgar writes diminuendo molto across the winds and strings at the close of the G minor Andante. The flutes and oboes stop first, then the bassoons and horns. The basses are silent, and the orchestral cellos hold a low note beneath the soloist’s last upward phrase and its long pause.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 86: successive wind releases, silent double basses, held orchestral cellos and the solo cello’s final phrase.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 82–86, rehearsal figures 52–54: solo cello, the orchestral answer and the return of the opening solo.

timeline.note: The solo cello plays above divided violas and a held note in the other cellos (p. 82).
All the cellos take up the tune with violas and basses; wind replies join them before the violins enter (pp. 82–83).
Divided violins join the melody over a quiet timpani roll and wind chords (p. 83).
Woodwind phrases are set around the long violin melody (p. 84).
The violins play on their G strings above lower wind chords (p. 85).
Woodwinds join the rising strings; trumpets and trombones do not play (pp. 85–86).
Elgar wrote dim. molto as the winds stop and the cello returns to its solo (p. 86).
Solo cello repeats its opening phrase over divided violas and held cello notes (p. 86).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
